## Paper

## Abstract

Daratumumab is approved for patients with multiple myeloma (MM) and high-risk
smoldering MM (HR-SMM). However, HR-SMM is often as genomically complex as MM,
suggesting it may be too advanced for single-agent intervention. We report on a Phase II
trial of single-agent daratumumab in patients with earlier-stage disease, including high-
risk monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and low-risk SMM, to test if
earlier treatment can induce deep responses and prevent progression to MM (D-
PRISM/NCT03236428, n = 41). As primary outcome, the rate of Very Good Partial
Response or better is 17% (95% CI: 7-32), which is comparable to what was observed in
HR-SMM and does not meet the study’s primary endpoint. The overall response rate is
54%, with two patients developing MM and 51% biochemical progression. Grade 3 or
higher toxicities include hypertension (7%), diarrhea (2%), flu-like symptoms (2%), and
headache (2%). Genomic and immune variables associated with biochemical progression
are identified in exploratory analyses leveraging whole-genome and single-cell RNA-
sequencing. This study demonstrates that, although less effective than expected,
daratumumab is safe and can induce deep responses in certain early-stage patients,
highlighting the importance of adopting genomic and immune profiling to improve patient
selection and maximize the benefit/risk ratio in trials of early intervention.

---

## Introduction

Precursor plasma cell disorders, including monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined
significance (MGUS) and smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM), exhibit a variable risk of
progression to symptomatic multiple myeloma (MM), ranging from 1% per year for MGUS
to up to ~50% in 2 years for patients with high-risk SMM (HR-SMM)1-5. MGUS is present
in approximately 4% of people over the age of 50, and has higher prevalence in older
individuals, Black individuals, and individuals with a family history of blood cancer1,2,4,6-11.
Features associated with high-risk MGUS (HR-MGUS) include non-IgG paraprotein,
serum M protein concentration of > 1.5 g/dl, and an abnormal free light chain (FLC) ratio,
and these patients carry a lifetime risk of progression to MM estimated at 37 - 58% at 20
years12,13. On the other hand, high-risk SMM can be defined by various criteria, including
the 2/20/20 model and the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) risk score
tool14. While low risk SMM (LR-SMM) patients may not be at immediate risk of
progression, approximately 50% will progress to overt MM at 10 years15. Additional high-
risk features that reflect disease biology, including cytogenetics, are currently under
investigation with promising results16-23.
Currently, the standard approach for patients with MGUS/SMM is observation until
progression24-26. However, early treatment with lenalidomide has shown benefit compared
to observation in two Phase III trials in patients with HR-SMM27-29. More recently, the
Phase III AQUILA trial demonstrated significant improvement in progression-free survival
(PFS) and overall survival (OS) with single-agent daratumumab compared to observation
in patients with HR-SMM30,31. On the basis of these results, daratumumab monotherapy
was recently approved for patients with HR-SMM in Europe and the US.
A key question remains whether the HR-SMM stage is already too advanced for a
single-drug intervention, as these patients exhibit genomic features that resemble those
seen in MM32-34. Several trials using intensive regimens in HR-SMM have failed to show
significantly different response rates compared to those observed in newly diagnosed MM
(NDMM). Examples of this include the GEM-CESAR trial, which studied the regimen of
carfilzomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone (KRD) and autologous stem cell
transplantation in HR-SMM, and demonstrated a complete response rate (CR) of 64%35.
Similarly, a single-arm trial of KRD demonstrated a CR rate of 75.9% and a trial of
ixazomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone demonstrated a CR rate of 31% in HR-
SMM36,37. This leads to the hypothesis that perhaps even earlier interventions at a lower-
risk disease state may be necessary to induce deeper responses and long-term remission
in certain patients with precursor conditions36,38. Another key challenge for the optimal
treatment of early-stage patients remains the identification of patients who are more likely
to benefit32-34,39. While the risk of progression of LR-SMM to overt myeloma is estimated
at 6.2% at 2 years per the 2/20/20 model, all patients with SMM carry a lifetime risk of
MM14. While there is general agreement that there is a need for tools that measure
disease biology and the state of the patient’s immune system in order to more accurately
predict who is likely to progress, it is not necessarily the case that those who are most
likely to progress when untreated are also the ones who are most likely to respond to
therapy, thus maximizing the benefit-risk ratio. For example, genomic variables that
predict a higher risk of progression to MM in patients with SMM, such as KRAS mutations,
are not predictors of response to therapy in patients with overt MM18,33. Therefore,
biomarkers to predict response to drugs, such as daratumumab, that may be used for
interception of progression in patients with SMM are needed to better drive clinical
decisions.
In this study, we aimed to assess whether single-agent daratumumab could induce
deep responses (i.e., Very Good Partial Response (VGPR) or better) and improve long-
term outcomes in patients with HR-MGUS and low-risk SMM (LR-SMM). Additionally, by
performing whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and single-cell RNA sequencing
(scRNAseq) of tumor and immune cells, we aimed to identify predictive biomarkers of
response to daratumumab monotherapy in early-stage patients, which following the
recent FDA approval may be critical for optimizing patient selection.

---

## Results

Efficacy and safety of single-agent daratumumab in patients with HR-MGUS and
LR-SMM
Between January 2018 and February 2020, 41 patients were enrolled on this study and
received therapy (Figure 1A). Patient baseline characteristics are summarized in
Supplementary Table 1 and Figure 1B. Most patients (n=36/41; 88%) had LR-SMM,
and 5 patients (12%) had HR-MGUS. Per the 2/20/20 criteria for patients with SMM
(n=36), 22 patients had LR-SMM (54%), 12 had IR-SMM (29%), and 2 (5%) had HR-
SMM. In total, 39/41 patients (95%) completed 20 cycles of therapy as per the protocol.
Two patients discontinued therapy early due to withdrawal of consent (one after 6 cycles
and one after 16 cycles).
When considering FISH results obtained at baseline, primary cytogenetic
abnormalities were detected in only 16 out of 41 patients (39%). In contrast, all 19 patients
(100%, 95% CI: 82-100) profiled at baseline with scRNAseq of tumor cells (n=17) or WGS
(n=14) were successfully classified. Furthermore, scRNAseq and WGS detected
additional secondary high-risk abnormalities (1q+, n=1; del13q, n=4). To enable
cytogenetic analyses, we allowed extrapolation of FISH results from any point during the
course of disease for primary cytogenetic abnormalities and any point prior to treatment
administration for secondary abnormalities, and successfully classified a total of 38
patients (93%, 95% CI: 80-98). By combining all results, we classified a total of 39/41
patients (95%, 95% CI: 83-99), whom we could assess for high-risk cytogenetics (Figure
1B). High-risk cytogenetics, as defined by the IMWG (i.e., considering t(4;14), t(14;16),
1q+, and del13q), were present in 14/39 patients (36%, 95% CI: 22-53)14.
Adverse events are detailed in Table 1. The most common toxicities of any grade
were fatigue (n = 24/41; 59%), cough (n = 19/41; 46%), nasal congestion (n = 17/41;
41%), headache (n = 14/41; 34%), nausea (n = 13/41; 32%), and leukopenia (n = 13/41;
32%). Grade 3 or higher toxicities included hypertension (n = 3/41; 7%), diarrhea (n =
1/41; 2%), flu-like symptoms (n = 1/41; 2%), and headache (n = 1/41; 2%). Upper
respiratory infections (URI) occurred in 9 patients (22%), with 10% of patients developing
grade 2 URIs. Neutropenia was seen in 12 patients (29%), with 7 (17%) experiencing
grade 2 neutropenia. There were no grade 3 neutropenias or grade 3 infections. No
patients developed secondary hematologic malignancies at a median follow-up of ~5
years. One patient developed a new primary cancer (breast cancer).
The overall response rate (ORR) defined as partial response (PR) or better was
54% (n=22/41; 95% CI: 37-69%; 90% CI: 40-67%). Seven patients achieved a best
overall response of VGPR or better (17%; 95% CI: 7-32%; 90% CI: 8-30%). Best overall
responses were complete response (CR, n = 4/41; 10%; 95% CI: 3-23%), VGPR (n =
3/41; 7%; 95% CI: 2-20%), PR (n = 15/41; 37%; 95% CI: 22-53%), or minor response
(MR, n = 12/41; 29%; 95% CI: 16-46%) (Table 2, Figure 1C). Seven patients did not
respond.
Progression-free and overall survival post-treatment with daratumumab in patients
with HR-MGUS and LR-SMM
The median follow-up for all 41 patients was 63.5 months (range, 6.7-79.8). Median OS
was not reached (NR), and OS was 100% at 5 years of follow-up (Figure 2A). As of
December 2024, 25 patients remained on follow-up. Overall, two patients progressed to
MM and in both cases, progression was diagnosed based on the SLiM criteria (Figure
2B)5. One of the 2 patients was noted to have 60% plasmacytosis on their end of
treatment (EOT) BM biopsy and subsequently began induction therapy. The other patient
was noted to have a FLC ratio of >100 at follow-up visit 3 and began induction therapy.
No patients developed symptomatic MM.
Twenty-one patients (51%, 95% CI: 35-67) developSed biochemical progression
based on the IMWG criteria40. The median biochemical PFS was 59.5 (range: 5.5-76.3)
months (Figure 2C). Six patients developed biochemical progression while on therapy,
while 15 patients developed it after completing therapy, with four patients developing it
within 1 year of completing therapy. No patients discontinued trial therapy due to
progression. Biochemical progressors demonstrated continuous gradual increase in M-
spike levels and involved:uninvolved FLC ratios over time (Figure 2D,E).
The median duration of response for patients who achieved PR or better was 64.8
months (Figure 2F). Out of the 21 patients who developed biochemical progression, one
patient started therapy on an HR-SMM protocol as they subsequently met 2/20/20 criteria
for HR-SMM, while another patient met the SLiM criteria for progression, as described
above, and began induction therapy. Nineteen patients had not started subsequent
therapy at the time of their last follow-up.
Depth of response and high-risk cytogenetics associated with biochemical PFS in
response to daratumumab
Next, we searched for variables that can predict biochemical PFS in our patients. There
was no difference in biochemical PFS by stage (HR-MGUS vs LR-SMM, two-sided log-
rank, p=0.66; 2/20/20 HR-SMM vs LR-SMM, p=0.45; 2/20/20 HR-SMM vs IR-SMM,
p=0.48) and neither M-spike levels nor BM infiltration were associated with biochemical
PFS on univariate analysis (p=0.22 & p=0.39, respectively)14. While there was no
difference in SLiM-CRAB PFS, biochemical PFS was significantly longer in patients who
achieved VGPR or better (NR vs 52.2 months; two-sided log-rank, p=0.014) and duration
of response was also longer, although this comparison did not reach statistical
significance (two-sided log-rank, p=0.075) (Figure 3A-C).
While the impact of high-risk cytogenetics, as defined by the IMWG, on SLiM-
CRAB PFS could not be assessed due to low power, biochemical PFS was significantly
longer in patients with SMM and standard vs high-risk cytogenetics by IMWG (NR vs 49.2
months; two-sided log-rank, p=0.037) (Figure 4A,B). To determine if other cytogenetic
abnormalities may be more predictive in the setting of daratumumab monotherapy, we
tested recurrent abnormalities that were present in at least 2 patients (Figure 4C).
Interestingly, we found that the presence of t(11;14) was associated with significantly
longer biochemical PFS (two-sided Wald p = 0.016 & two-sided log-rank p=0.0029)
(Figure 4D). In contrast, the presence of t(4;14) was associated with shorter biochemical
PFS (two-sided Wald p=0.0046 & two-sided log-rank p < 0.001) (Figure 4E). The
presence of t(4;14) is considered a high-risk factor in both treatment-naïve patients with
SMM, as well as patients with overt MM who receive therapy. On the other hand, the
presence of t(11;14) is not associated with superior outcomes in treatment-naïve patients
with SMM or patients with overt disease who receive therapy. Thus, the observed
association of t(11;14) with response to daratumumab may be related to its administration
as monotherapy instead of in combination with other agents or its administration earlier
on in the course of disease.
Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals immune biomarkers of response to
daratumumab monotherapy in patients with HR-MGUS and LR-SMM
To explore how the immune system may influence response to daratumumab
monotherapy in this patient population, we performed scRNAseq on 48 CD138-negative
and 18 CD138-positive BM mononuclear cell samples from 36 patients (biochemical
progressors (P), n=18; non-biochemical progressors (NP), n=16; patients who
discontinued treatment, n=2). Another 6 patients (P, n=3; NP, n=3) also had samples
drawn at EOT to monitor immune cell dynamics post-therapy (Supplementary Table 2).
Notably, among progressors, 8 patients progressed within ~24 months from treatment
initiation (early progressors), while the remaining patients (n=10) progressed after ~45
months (late progressors). In total, we profiled 71,771 BM immune cells, including 37,734
T cells, 10,338 NK cells, 5,422 B cells, 16,277 monocytes, and 2,000 dendritic cells
(Figure 5A).
First, we compared the proportions of all immune cell types (n=20) between
progressors (n=18) and non-progressors (n=16). Interestingly, biochemical progressors
had significantly higher proportions of CD56dim NK cells at baseline compared to non-
progressors (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum, q=0.0364) (Figure 5B). No such difference
was observed between early vs late progressors (p=0.275). To ensure our results were
not confounded by differences in target antigen expression by tumor cells, we compared
the proportion of CD38-expressing (>0.1) tumor cells between groups and observed no
association with biochemical progression (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum, p=0.613)
(Figure 5C). Furthermore, no significant difference in tumor burden was observed
between progressors and non-progressors (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum, p=0.644 and
p=0.581 for BM infiltration and M-spike, respectively). Lastly, and in line with prior
observations, the proportion of CD38-expressing (>0.1) CD56dim NK cells decreased
significantly post-treatment (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, p=0.00216), but with no
difference between progressors (n=3) and non-progressors (n=3), suggesting that NK cell
fratricide due to CD38 expression may not be associated with response in this setting
(Figure 5D)41.
To understand how the baseline phenotype of CD56dim NK cells differs between
progressors and non-progressors, we performed differential expression analysis after
downsampling to ensure equal numbers of cells were contributed by each patient within
each group and equal numbers of cells were compared across groups (P, n=18; NP,
n=11; 396 cells per group). We observed significantly higher levels of FCER1G in
CD56dim NK cells of non-progressors compared to progressors and in late compared to
early progressors (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum, q < 0.05) (Figure 5E,F).

---

## Methods

D-PRISM is a single-arm, Phase II study using single-agent daratumumab in patients with
HR-MGUS and LR-SMM (D-PRISM; NCT03236428, posted 1 August 2017). The trial
protocol was approved by the Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center Institutional Review
Board (#17-212) and is provided in the Supplementary Information file. Patient samples
were banked under this protocol for correlative studies. All participants provided written
informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Patient selection was
blind to the participant’s sex and gender.
Eligibility Criteria
Eligibility criteria for patients with HR-MGUS included <10% plasmacytosis and < 3 g/dL
M-spike in the serum along with at least 2 of the following 3 criteria: abnormal serum FLC
ratio (<0.26 or > 1.65), M protein ≥ 1.5 g/dL or non-IgG M protein (including IgA). Low-
risk SMM was defined as having only 1 of the following criteria: monoclonal protein ≥ 3
g/dL, ≥ 10% BM plasmacytosis, or sFLC ratio < 0.125 or > 8. Patients who met SLiM-
CRAB criteria were excluded5.
Treatment Regimen
A treatment cycle was defined as 4 weeks in length. All patients received daratumumab
dosed at 16 mg/kg intravenously for each four-week cycle for up to 20 cycles. During
Cycles 1 and 2, patients received daratumumab weekly. During cycles 3 through 6,
daratumumab was administered every 2 weeks. During cycles 7 through 20,
daratumumab was administered every 4 weeks. Assessments of disease and progression
were performed at the beginning of each cycle, at the end of treatment, and every 3 or 6
months thereafter. Patients were to be followed for up to five years after the
discontinuation of therapy.
Objectives and End Points
The primary objective of this trial was to determine the proportion of patients who achieve
VGPR or better after 20 cycles of therapy. Response was determined according to the
IMWG criteria52. Secondary objectives included the following: 1) assess the duration of
response; 2) assess the safety of the agent in this patient population; 3) assess if baseline
immune features can predict response or progression, 4) assess changes in the immune
microenvironment in HR-MGUS and LR-SMM patients during the study; 5) assess the
association between immune changes and progression to SMM or MM; and 6) assess
the rate of secondary hematologic malignancies.
Statistics & Reproducibility
The study aimed to enroll 50 patients, however due to the COVID-19 pandemic that
occurred during the trial enrollment period, enrollment was ended early with 41 patients
enrolled. The study was not randomized and thus, the investigators were not blinded.
According to the study protocol, the criterion to determine whether the treatment is
promising was for the lower limit of the two-sided 90% binomial confidence interval for the
deep response rate (i.e., VGPR or better) to be at least 50%. In practice, both 90%
confidence intervals and 95% confidence intervals were reported for ORR and the rate of
VGPR or better. Patients who received any amount of study treatment were evaluable for
safety and toxicity analyses from the time of their first dose. Patients who had measurable
disease, received at least one cycle of therapy, and had their disease re-evaluated were
considered evaluable for response. Patients who showed objective disease progression
prior to removal from the study were also considered evaluable.
No data was excluded from analysis, unless explicitly stated in the manuscript and
figure legend. For example, analyses on genomic biomarkers of progression were
conducted in patients with SMM who had cytogenetic data available, thus excluding
patients with MGUS and a single patient with SMM and no cytogenetic information.
Progression-free survival was measured from the date of registration to the date
of documentation of progressive disease (SLiM-CRAB or biochemical progression) or
death from any cause and censored for those alive and free from progression. According
to the SLiM-CRAB criteria, a diagnosis of MM was made if ≥ 60% clonal plasma cells
were detected in the BM, the involved:uninvolved FLC ratio was ≥ 100, >1 focal lesion
was detected on MRI, or patients developed CRAB symptoms5. Time-to-event endpoints
were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Median follow-up was calculated using
the reverse Kaplan-Meier method. Clinical responses to study treatment were reported
as proportions with 95% exact binomial confidence intervals. Continuous measures were
summarized by their median and range, and categorical variables were summarized as
proportions. Response outcomes and other categorical variables were tested for
association with continuous variables using two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests or to other
categorical variables using two-sided Fisher’s exact tests. Statistical analyses of clinical
data were performed using R (v4.4.2; 2024-10-31).
No sex-based or gender-based analyses were conducted in this study, as such
analyses were not part of the study protocol. Self-reported sex information is available for
participants in the scRNAseq cohort in the study’s dbGaP site (for access to dbGaP,
please, see Data Availability).
Non-preplanned exploratory outcomes
Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) data and analysis
Bone marrow (BM) aspirates from 36 patients enrolled on the trial were collected at
baseline (n=36) and EOT (n=6). Bone marrow mononuclear cells were isolated using
Ficoll and subjected to CD138 selection using AutoMACS (Miltenyi), followed by
cryopreservation in Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS), supplemented with 10% Dimethyl
Sulfoxide (DMSO). Cryopreserved CD138-negative cells (n=48) from 36 individuals and
CD138-positive cells (n=18) from 17 individuals were thawed and encapsulated on a
Chromium Controller, according to the manufacturer’s instructions (10X Genomics).
Gene expression libraries were prepared using Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 5’
Reagent Kits (v2, Dual Index) and Library Construction Kits (10X Genomics). For tumor
samples, B cell receptor (BCR) libraries were also constructed using Chromium Single
Cell Human BCR Amplification Kits and Library Construction Kits, according to the
manufacturer’s instructions (10X Genomics). Libraries were sequenced on NovaSeq
S6000 instruments at the Genomics Platform of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard
(Cambridge, MA).
FASTQ files were demultiplexed, and count matrices were produced using
CellRanger (v6.0.1), and downstream analyses were conducted using R (v4.2.2) and
Seurat (v5.1.0)53,54. Immune cells were annotated using established immune cell
expression markers and differential expression analysis, as is standard in the
field44,45,55,56. Red blood cells and plasma cells identified in the CD138-negative samples
were discarded, resulting in a total of 20 immune cell types used for downstream
analyses. Tumor cells were identified on the basis of expressing markers of malignancy
(e.g., NCAM1, CCND1, etc.) and exhibiting monoclonal expansion in the BCR data44,56-
58.
Immune cell proportions were computed by dividing the cell count of a cell type in
a sample by the sample’s total immune cell count. Two patients who discontinued
treatment were excluded from downstream analyses related to progression. The
remaining patients had at least 200 immune cells detected and were included in
downstream analyses (n=34). Immune cell proportions for all cell types (n=20) were
compared between biochemical progressors (n=18) and non-progressors (n=16), or early
(n=8) and late biochemical progressors (n=10), using two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests,
and p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method (a=0.05). The
proportion of CD38-expressing tumor cells and CD56dim NK cells was determined by
computing the proportion of cells with normalized CD38 expression > 0.1. For 6 patients
with EOT samples available, the proportion of CD38-expressing CD56dim NK cells was
compared between baseline and EOT timepoints by a two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-
rank test.
Differential expression analysis was conducted using two-sided Wilcoxon rank-
sum tests to compare the baseline expression profile of CD56dim NK cells between
biochemical progressors (n=18) and non-progressors (n=11), or early (n=8) and late
biochemical progressors (n=10). Only patients with at least 20 CD56dim NK cells at
baseline were considered for these analyses. To balance the number of cells compared
between groups as well as the number of cells contributed by each individual, we
downsampled 396 cells per group for biochemical progressors (18 patients, 22 cells each)
versus non-progressors (11 patients, 36 cells each) analysis and 280 cells per group for
early (8 patients, 35 cells each) versus late biochemical progressors (10 patients, 28 cells
each) analysis. Lastly, we filtered for genes with more than 3 counts in at least 10 cells.
P-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method (a=0.05).
Whole genome sequencing (WGS) of tumor samples
Whole genome sequencing was performed on bone marrow CD138+ cells (tumor) and
matched peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC; normal). Genomic DNA was
extracted using the Monarch Genomic DNA Purification Kit (New England Biolabs), and
libraries were prepared using the NEBNext Ultra II FS DNA Library Prep Kit (New England
Biolabs) with unique dual-index adapters (NEBNext Multiplex Oligos) and sequenced at
the Genomics Platform of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard (Cambridge, MA).
Sequencing reads were aligned to GRCh38, and the Getz Lab WGS processing and
analysis pipeline was deployed, as previously described33,59.
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and cytogenetic classification analyses
Results from clinical-grade FISH testing were extracted from medical records and
reviewed for accuracy by three independent data collectors. To maximize the contribution
of FISH to our cytogenetic classification, we allowed extrapolation of FISH results for
primary cytogenetic abnormalities only (i.e., patients were considered positive for primary
IgH translocations and hyperdiploidy, if they were positive by FISH at any point during the

explains our use of a 90% confidence interval in the study protocol and our original reporting of
ORR results. Of note, as discussed in the Methods section, enrollment was ended early due to
the COVID-19 pandemic, with a cohort of 41 patients, instead of our originally planned number of
50 (Revised manuscript, p. 8).
To address the reviewer’s concern, we decided to report the more stringent 95%
confidence intervals instead for all endpoints to ensure consistence across the manuscript, but
additionally reported 90% confidence intervals for ORR and deep response rate to align with the
study protocol (for ORR results, please see Revised manuscript, p. 4).
2. In Figure 5, although the statistical methods section does not mention it, you appear to have
applied a Benjamini–Hochberg procedure for multiple-comparison adjustment. Please, clarify for
which specific set of multiple tests this correction was applied, and explicitly state the significance
level used after adjustment.
We thank the reviewer for their comment. The use of Benjamini-Hochberg for multiple
hypotheses testing correction is explicitly mentioned in our Methods section pertaining to single-
cell RNA-seq analysis where it was used. Specifically, it was employed wherever multiple
hypotheses were tested: (i) Figure 5B: all immune cell types (n=20) were tested for an association
with biochemical progression and CD56dim NK cells were the only population passing the
significance threshold, which is set at 0.05 throughout analysis, as mentioned in the Methods
section; (ii) Figures 5E & 5F: genes that pass the criteria discussed in the Methods section (n=660

the Benjamini-Hochberg approach; genes with an adjusted p-value (q-value) of < 0.05 were
labeled, as described in the Figure legend.
3. In Figure 5B, the notation “q” is used — is this intended to denote an adjusted p-value (i.e., q-

This is correct, q-value refers to the BH-adjusted p-value. Specifically, we compared cell
type proportions between biochemical progressors and non-progressors for all 20 immune cell
populations, and corrected those p-values using the BH approach. Only CD56dim NK cells
passed our alpha threshold of 0.05 and were thus visualized. This is explained in our Results
section (Revised manuscript, p. 5):
“First, we compared the proportions of all immune cell types (n=20) between progressors (n=18)
and non-progressors (n=16). Interestingly, biochemical progressors had significantly higher
proportions of CD56dim NK cells at baseline compared to non-progressors (two-sided Wilcoxon
rank-sum, q=0.0364) (Figure 5B).”
4. The manuscript mentions 95% confidence intervals for the Kaplan–Meier curves. Please
indicate clearly where these intervals were actually used in the analysis or figures, and revise the
statistical methods section to focus on the analyses that were actually performed in this study.
We thank the reviewer for their feedback; since we did not visualize 95% confidence
intervals in our KM plots, we have removed the corresponding statement from the Methods
section of our revised manuscript.

## Paper

## Abstract

Daratumumab is approved for patients with multiple myeloma (MM) and high-risk
smoldering MM (HR-SMM). However, HR-SMM is often as genomically complex as MM,
suggesting it may be too advanced for single-agent intervention. We report on a Phase II
trial of single-agent daratumumab in patients with earlier-stage disease, including high-
risk monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and low-risk SMM, to test if
earlier treatment can induce deep responses and prevent progression to MM (D-
PRISM/NCT03236428, n = 41). As primary outcome, the rate of Very Good Partial
Response or better is 17% (95% CI: 7-32), which is comparable to what was observed in
HR-SMM and does not meet the study’s primary endpoint. The overall response rate is
54%, with two patients developing MM and 51% biochemical progression. Grade 3 or
higher toxicities include hypertension (7%), diarrhea (2%), flu-like symptoms (2%), and
headache (2%). Genomic and immune variables associated with biochemical progression
are identified in exploratory analyses leveraging whole-genome and single-cell RNA-
sequencing. This study demonstrates that, although less effective than expected,
daratumumab is safe and can induce deep responses in certain early-stage patients,
highlighting the importance of adopting genomic and immune profiling to improve patient
selection and maximize the benefit/risk ratio in trials of early intervention.

---

## Introduction

Precursor plasma cell disorders, including monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined
significance (MGUS) and smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM), exhibit a variable risk of
progression to symptomatic multiple myeloma (MM), ranging from 1% per year for MGUS
to up to ~50% in 2 years for patients with high-risk SMM (HR-SMM)1-5. MGUS is present
in approximately 4% of people over the age of 50, and has higher prevalence in older
individuals, Black individuals, and individuals with a family history of blood cancer1,2,4,6-11.
Features associated with high-risk MGUS (HR-MGUS) include non-IgG paraprotein,
serum M protein concentration of > 1.5 g/dl, and an abnormal free light chain (FLC) ratio,
and these patients carry a lifetime risk of progression to MM estimated at 37 - 58% at 20
years12,13. On the other hand, high-risk SMM can be defined by various criteria, including
the 2/20/20 model and the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) risk score
tool14. While low risk SMM (LR-SMM) patients may not be at immediate risk of
progression, approximately 50% will progress to overt MM at 10 years15. Additional high-
risk features that reflect disease biology, including cytogenetics, are currently under
investigation with promising results16-23.
Currently, the standard approach for patients with MGUS/SMM is observation until
progression24-26. However, early treatment with lenalidomide has shown benefit compared
to observation in two Phase III trials in patients with HR-SMM27-29. More recently, the
Phase III AQUILA trial demonstrated significant improvement in progression-free survival
(PFS) and overall survival (OS) with single-agent daratumumab compared to observation
in patients with HR-SMM30,31. On the basis of these results, daratumumab monotherapy
was recently approved for patients with HR-SMM in Europe and the US.
A key question remains whether the HR-SMM stage is already too advanced for a
single-drug intervention, as these patients exhibit genomic features that resemble those
seen in MM32-34. Several trials using intensive regimens in HR-SMM have failed to show
significantly different response rates compared to those observed in newly diagnosed MM
(NDMM). Examples of this include the GEM-CESAR trial, which studied the regimen of
carfilzomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone (KRD) and autologous stem cell
transplantation in HR-SMM, and demonstrated a complete response rate (CR) of 64%35.
Similarly, a single-arm trial of KRD demonstrated a CR rate of 75.9% and a trial of
ixazomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone demonstrated a CR rate of 31% in HR-
SMM36,37. This leads to the hypothesis that perhaps even earlier interventions at a lower-
risk disease state may be necessary to induce deeper responses and long-term remission
in certain patients with precursor conditions36,38. Another key challenge for the optimal
treatment of early-stage patients remains the identification of patients who are more likely
to benefit32-34,39. While the risk of progression of LR-SMM to overt myeloma is estimated
at 6.2% at 2 years per the 2/20/20 model, all patients with SMM carry a lifetime risk of
MM14. While there is general agreement that there is a need for tools that measure
disease biology and the state of the patient’s immune system in order to more accurately
predict who is likely to progress, it is not necessarily the case that those who are most
likely to progress when untreated are also the ones who are most likely to respond to
therapy, thus maximizing the benefit-risk ratio. For example, genomic variables that
predict a higher risk of progression to MM in patients with SMM, such as KRAS mutations,
are not predictors of response to therapy in patients with overt MM18,33. Therefore,
biomarkers to predict response to drugs, such as daratumumab, that may be used for
interception of progression in patients with SMM are needed to better drive clinical
decisions.
In this study, we aimed to assess whether single-agent daratumumab could induce
deep responses (i.e., Very Good Partial Response (VGPR) or better) and improve long-
term outcomes in patients with HR-MGUS and low-risk SMM (LR-SMM). Additionally, by
performing whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and single-cell RNA sequencing
(scRNAseq) of tumor and immune cells, we aimed to identify predictive biomarkers of
response to daratumumab monotherapy in early-stage patients, which following the
recent FDA approval may be critical for optimizing patient selection.

---

## Results

Efficacy and safety of single-agent daratumumab in patients with HR-MGUS and
LR-SMM
Between January 2018 and February 2020, 41 patients were enrolled on this study and
received therapy (Figure 1A). Patient baseline characteristics are summarized in
Supplementary Table 1 and Figure 1B. Most patients (n=36/41; 88%) had LR-SMM,
and 5 patients (12%) had HR-MGUS. Per the 2/20/20 criteria for patients with SMM
(n=36), 22 patients had LR-SMM (54%), 12 had IR-SMM (29%), and 2 (5%) had HR-
SMM. In total, 39/41 patients (95%) completed 20 cycles of therapy as per the protocol.
Two patients discontinued therapy early due to withdrawal of consent (one after 6 cycles
and one after 16 cycles).
When considering FISH results obtained at baseline, primary cytogenetic
abnormalities were detected in only 16 out of 41 patients (39%). In contrast, all 19 patients
(100%, 95% CI: 82-100) profiled at baseline with scRNAseq of tumor cells (n=17) or WGS
(n=14) were successfully classified. Furthermore, scRNAseq and WGS detected
additional secondary high-risk abnormalities (1q+, n=1; del13q, n=4). To enable
cytogenetic analyses, we allowed extrapolation of FISH results from any point during the
course of disease for primary cytogenetic abnormalities and any point prior to treatment
administration for secondary abnormalities, and successfully classified a total of 38
patients (93%, 95% CI: 80-98). By combining all results, we classified a total of 39/41
patients (95%, 95% CI: 83-99), whom we could assess for high-risk cytogenetics (Figure
1B). High-risk cytogenetics, as defined by the IMWG (i.e., considering t(4;14), t(14;16),
1q+, and del13q), were present in 14/39 patients (36%, 95% CI: 22-53)14.
Adverse events are detailed in Table 1. The most common toxicities of any grade
were fatigue (n = 24/41; 59%), cough (n = 19/41; 46%), nasal congestion (n = 17/41;
41%), headache (n = 14/41; 34%), nausea (n = 13/41; 32%), and leukopenia (n = 13/41;
32%). Grade 3 or higher toxicities included hypertension (n = 3/41; 7%), diarrhea (n =
1/41; 2%), flu-like symptoms (n = 1/41; 2%), and headache (n = 1/41; 2%). Upper
respiratory infections (URI) occurred in 9 patients (22%), with 10% of patients developing
grade 2 URIs. Neutropenia was seen in 12 patients (29%), with 7 (17%) experiencing
grade 2 neutropenia. There were no grade 3 neutropenias or grade 3 infections. No
patients developed secondary hematologic malignancies at a median follow-up of ~5
years. One patient developed a new primary cancer (breast cancer).
The overall response rate (ORR) defined as partial response (PR) or better was
54% (n=22/41; 95% CI: 37-69%; 90% CI: 40-67%). Seven patients achieved a best
overall response of VGPR or better (17%; 95% CI: 7-32%; 90% CI: 8-30%). Best overall
responses were complete response (CR, n = 4/41; 10%; 95% CI: 3-23%), VGPR (n =
3/41; 7%; 95% CI: 2-20%), PR (n = 15/41; 37%; 95% CI: 22-53%), or minor response
(MR, n = 12/41; 29%; 95% CI: 16-46%) (Table 2, Figure 1C). Seven patients did not
respond.
Progression-free and overall survival post-treatment with daratumumab in patients
with HR-MGUS and LR-SMM
The median follow-up for all 41 patients was 63.5 months (range, 6.7-79.8). Median OS
was not reached (NR), and OS was 100% at 5 years of follow-up (Figure 2A). As of
December 2024, 25 patients remained on follow-up. Overall, two patients progressed to
MM and in both cases, progression was diagnosed based on the SLiM criteria (Figure
2B)5. One of the 2 patients was noted to have 60% plasmacytosis on their end of
treatment (EOT) BM biopsy and subsequently began induction therapy. The other patient
was noted to have a FLC ratio of >100 at follow-up visit 3 and began induction therapy.
No patients developed symptomatic MM.
Twenty-one patients (51%, 95% CI: 35-67) developSed biochemical progression
based on the IMWG criteria40. The median biochemical PFS was 59.5 (range: 5.5-76.3)
months (Figure 2C). Six patients developed biochemical progression while on therapy,
while 15 patients developed it after completing therapy, with four patients developing it
within 1 year of completing therapy. No patients discontinued trial therapy due to
progression. Biochemical progressors demonstrated continuous gradual increase in M-
spike levels and involved:uninvolved FLC ratios over time (Figure 2D,E).
The median duration of response for patients who achieved PR or better was 64.8
months (Figure 2F). Out of the 21 patients who developed biochemical progression, one
patient started therapy on an HR-SMM protocol as they subsequently met 2/20/20 criteria
for HR-SMM, while another patient met the SLiM criteria for progression, as described
above, and began induction therapy. Nineteen patients had not started subsequent
therapy at the time of their last follow-up.
Depth of response and high-risk cytogenetics associated with biochemical PFS in
response to daratumumab
Next, we searched for variables that can predict biochemical PFS in our patients. There
was no difference in biochemical PFS by stage (HR-MGUS vs LR-SMM, two-sided log-
rank, p=0.66; 2/20/20 HR-SMM vs LR-SMM, p=0.45; 2/20/20 HR-SMM vs IR-SMM,
p=0.48) and neither M-spike levels nor BM infiltration were associated with biochemical
PFS on univariate analysis (p=0.22 & p=0.39, respectively)14. While there was no
difference in SLiM-CRAB PFS, biochemical PFS was significantly longer in patients who
achieved VGPR or better (NR vs 52.2 months; two-sided log-rank, p=0.014) and duration
of response was also longer, although this comparison did not reach statistical
significance (two-sided log-rank, p=0.075) (Figure 3A-C).
While the impact of high-risk cytogenetics, as defined by the IMWG, on SLiM-
CRAB PFS could not be assessed due to low power, biochemical PFS was significantly
longer in patients with SMM and standard vs high-risk cytogenetics by IMWG (NR vs 49.2
months; two-sided log-rank, p=0.037) (Figure 4A,B). To determine if other cytogenetic
abnormalities may be more predictive in the setting of daratumumab monotherapy, we
tested recurrent abnormalities that were present in at least 2 patients (Figure 4C).
Interestingly, we found that the presence of t(11;14) was associated with significantly
longer biochemical PFS (two-sided Wald p = 0.016 & two-sided log-rank p=0.0029)
(Figure 4D). In contrast, the presence of t(4;14) was associated with shorter biochemical
PFS (two-sided Wald p=0.0046 & two-sided log-rank p < 0.001) (Figure 4E). The
presence of t(4;14) is considered a high-risk factor in both treatment-naïve patients with
SMM, as well as patients with overt MM who receive therapy. On the other hand, the
presence of t(11;14) is not associated with superior outcomes in treatment-naïve patients
with SMM or patients with overt disease who receive therapy. Thus, the observed
association of t(11;14) with response to daratumumab may be related to its administration
as monotherapy instead of in combination with other agents or its administration earlier
on in the course of disease.
Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals immune biomarkers of response to
daratumumab monotherapy in patients with HR-MGUS and LR-SMM
To explore how the immune system may influence response to daratumumab
monotherapy in this patient population, we performed scRNAseq on 48 CD138-negative
and 18 CD138-positive BM mononuclear cell samples from 36 patients (biochemical
progressors (P), n=18; non-biochemical progressors (NP), n=16; patients who
discontinued treatment, n=2). Another 6 patients (P, n=3; NP, n=3) also had samples
drawn at EOT to monitor immune cell dynamics post-therapy (Supplementary Table 2).
Notably, among progressors, 8 patients progressed within ~24 months from treatment
initiation (early progressors), while the remaining patients (n=10) progressed after ~45
months (late progressors). In total, we profiled 71,771 BM immune cells, including 37,734
T cells, 10,338 NK cells, 5,422 B cells, 16,277 monocytes, and 2,000 dendritic cells
(Figure 5A).
First, we compared the proportions of all immune cell types (n=20) between
progressors (n=18) and non-progressors (n=16). Interestingly, biochemical progressors
had significantly higher proportions of CD56dim NK cells at baseline compared to non-
progressors (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum, q=0.0364) (Figure 5B). No such difference
was observed between early vs late progressors (p=0.275). To ensure our results were
not confounded by differences in target antigen expression by tumor cells, we compared
the proportion of CD38-expressing (>0.1) tumor cells between groups and observed no
association with biochemical progression (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum, p=0.613)
(Figure 5C). Furthermore, no significant difference in tumor burden was observed
between progressors and non-progressors (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum, p=0.644 and
p=0.581 for BM infiltration and M-spike, respectively). Lastly, and in line with prior
observations, the proportion of CD38-expressing (>0.1) CD56dim NK cells decreased
significantly post-treatment (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, p=0.00216), but with no
difference between progressors (n=3) and non-progressors (n=3), suggesting that NK cell
fratricide due to CD38 expression may not be associated with response in this setting
(Figure 5D)41.
To understand how the baseline phenotype of CD56dim NK cells differs between
progressors and non-progressors, we performed differential expression analysis after
downsampling to ensure equal numbers of cells were contributed by each patient within
each group and equal numbers of cells were compared across groups (P, n=18; NP,
n=11; 396 cells per group). We observed significantly higher levels of FCER1G in
CD56dim NK cells of non-progressors compared to progressors and in late compared to
early progressors (two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum, q < 0.05) (Figure 5E,F).

---

## Methods

D-PRISM is a single-arm, Phase II study using single-agent daratumumab in patients with
HR-MGUS and LR-SMM (D-PRISM; NCT03236428, posted 1 August 2017). The trial
protocol was approved by the Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center Institutional Review
Board (#17-212) and is provided in the Supplementary Information file. Patient samples
were banked under this protocol for correlative studies. All participants provided written
informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Patient selection was
blind to the participant’s sex and gender.
Eligibility Criteria
Eligibility criteria for patients with HR-MGUS included <10% plasmacytosis and < 3 g/dL
M-spike in the serum along with at least 2 of the following 3 criteria: abnormal serum FLC
ratio (<0.26 or > 1.65), M protein ≥ 1.5 g/dL or non-IgG M protein (including IgA). Low-
risk SMM was defined as having only 1 of the following criteria: monoclonal protein ≥ 3
g/dL, ≥ 10% BM plasmacytosis, or sFLC ratio < 0.125 or > 8. Patients who met SLiM-
CRAB criteria were excluded5.
Treatment Regimen
A treatment cycle was defined as 4 weeks in length. All patients received daratumumab
dosed at 16 mg/kg intravenously for each four-week cycle for up to 20 cycles. During
Cycles 1 and 2, patients received daratumumab weekly. During cycles 3 through 6,
daratumumab was administered every 2 weeks. During cycles 7 through 20,
daratumumab was administered every 4 weeks. Assessments of disease and progression
were performed at the beginning of each cycle, at the end of treatment, and every 3 or 6
months thereafter. Patients were to be followed for up to five years after the
discontinuation of therapy.
Objectives and End Points
The primary objective of this trial was to determine the proportion of patients who achieve
VGPR or better after 20 cycles of therapy. Response was determined according to the
IMWG criteria52. Secondary objectives included the following: 1) assess the duration of
response; 2) assess the safety of the agent in this patient population; 3) assess if baseline
immune features can predict response or progression, 4) assess changes in the immune
microenvironment in HR-MGUS and LR-SMM patients during the study; 5) assess the
association between immune changes and progression to SMM or MM; and 6) assess
the rate of secondary hematologic malignancies.
Statistics & Reproducibility
The study aimed to enroll 50 patients, however due to the COVID-19 pandemic that
occurred during the trial enrollment period, enrollment was ended early with 41 patients
enrolled. The study was not randomized and thus, the investigators were not blinded.
According to the study protocol, the criterion to determine whether the treatment is
promising was for the lower limit of the two-sided 90% binomial confidence interval for the
deep response rate (i.e., VGPR or better) to be at least 50%. In practice, both 90%
confidence intervals and 95% confidence intervals were reported for ORR and the rate of
VGPR or better. Patients who received any amount of study treatment were evaluable for
safety and toxicity analyses from the time of their first dose. Patients who had measurable
disease, received at least one cycle of therapy, and had their disease re-evaluated were
considered evaluable for response. Patients who showed objective disease progression
prior to removal from the study were also considered evaluable.
No data was excluded from analysis, unless explicitly stated in the manuscript and
figure legend. For example, analyses on genomic biomarkers of progression were
conducted in patients with SMM who had cytogenetic data available, thus excluding
patients with MGUS and a single patient with SMM and no cytogenetic information.
Progression-free survival was measured from the date of registration to the date
of documentation of progressive disease (SLiM-CRAB or biochemical progression) or
death from any cause and censored for those alive and free from progression. According
to the SLiM-CRAB criteria, a diagnosis of MM was made if ≥ 60% clonal plasma cells
were detected in the BM, the involved:uninvolved FLC ratio was ≥ 100, >1 focal lesion
was detected on MRI, or patients developed CRAB symptoms5. Time-to-event endpoints
were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Median follow-up was calculated using
the reverse Kaplan-Meier method. Clinical responses to study treatment were reported
as proportions with 95% exact binomial confidence intervals. Continuous measures were
summarized by their median and range, and categorical variables were summarized as
proportions. Response outcomes and other categorical variables were tested for
association with continuous variables using two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests or to other
categorical variables using two-sided Fisher’s exact tests. Statistical analyses of clinical
data were performed using R (v4.4.2; 2024-10-31).
No sex-based or gender-based analyses were conducted in this study, as such
analyses were not part of the study protocol. Self-reported sex information is available for
participants in the scRNAseq cohort in the study’s dbGaP site (for access to dbGaP,
please, see Data Availability).
Non-preplanned exploratory outcomes
Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) data and analysis
Bone marrow (BM) aspirates from 36 patients enrolled on the trial were collected at
baseline (n=36) and EOT (n=6). Bone marrow mononuclear cells were isolated using
Ficoll and subjected to CD138 selection using AutoMACS (Miltenyi), followed by
cryopreservation in Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS), supplemented with 10% Dimethyl
Sulfoxide (DMSO). Cryopreserved CD138-negative cells (n=48) from 36 individuals and
CD138-positive cells (n=18) from 17 individuals were thawed and encapsulated on a
Chromium Controller, according to the manufacturer’s instructions (10X Genomics).
Gene expression libraries were prepared using Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 5’
Reagent Kits (v2, Dual Index) and Library Construction Kits (10X Genomics). For tumor
samples, B cell receptor (BCR) libraries were also constructed using Chromium Single
Cell Human BCR Amplification Kits and Library Construction Kits, according to the
manufacturer’s instructions (10X Genomics). Libraries were sequenced on NovaSeq
S6000 instruments at the Genomics Platform of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard
(Cambridge, MA).
FASTQ files were demultiplexed, and count matrices were produced using
CellRanger (v6.0.1), and downstream analyses were conducted using R (v4.2.2) and
Seurat (v5.1.0)53,54. Immune cells were annotated using established immune cell
expression markers and differential expression analysis, as is standard in the
field44,45,55,56. Red blood cells and plasma cells identified in the CD138-negative samples
were discarded, resulting in a total of 20 immune cell types used for downstream
analyses. Tumor cells were identified on the basis of expressing markers of malignancy
(e.g., NCAM1, CCND1, etc.) and exhibiting monoclonal expansion in the BCR data44,56-
58.
Immune cell proportions were computed by dividing the cell count of a cell type in
a sample by the sample’s total immune cell count. Two patients who discontinued
treatment were excluded from downstream analyses related to progression. The
remaining patients had at least 200 immune cells detected and were included in
downstream analyses (n=34). Immune cell proportions for all cell types (n=20) were
compared between biochemical progressors (n=18) and non-progressors (n=16), or early
(n=8) and late biochemical progressors (n=10), using two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests,
and p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method (a=0.05). The
proportion of CD38-expressing tumor cells and CD56dim NK cells was determined by
computing the proportion of cells with normalized CD38 expression > 0.1. For 6 patients
with EOT samples available, the proportion of CD38-expressing CD56dim NK cells was
compared between baseline and EOT timepoints by a two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-
rank test.
Differential expression analysis was conducted using two-sided Wilcoxon rank-
sum tests to compare the baseline expression profile of CD56dim NK cells between
biochemical progressors (n=18) and non-progressors (n=11), or early (n=8) and late
biochemical progressors (n=10). Only patients with at least 20 CD56dim NK cells at
baseline were considered for these analyses. To balance the number of cells compared
between groups as well as the number of cells contributed by each individual, we
downsampled 396 cells per group for biochemical progressors (18 patients, 22 cells each)
versus non-progressors (11 patients, 36 cells each) analysis and 280 cells per group for
early (8 patients, 35 cells each) versus late biochemical progressors (10 patients, 28 cells
each) analysis. Lastly, we filtered for genes with more than 3 counts in at least 10 cells.
P-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg method (a=0.05).
Whole genome sequencing (WGS) of tumor samples
Whole genome sequencing was performed on bone marrow CD138+ cells (tumor) and
matched peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC; normal). Genomic DNA was
extracted using the Monarch Genomic DNA Purification Kit (New England Biolabs), and
libraries were prepared using the NEBNext Ultra II FS DNA Library Prep Kit (New England
Biolabs) with unique dual-index adapters (NEBNext Multiplex Oligos) and sequenced at
the Genomics Platform of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard (Cambridge, MA).
Sequencing reads were aligned to GRCh38, and the Getz Lab WGS processing and
analysis pipeline was deployed, as previously described33,59.
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and cytogenetic classification analyses
Results from clinical-grade FISH testing were extracted from medical records and
reviewed for accuracy by three independent data collectors. To maximize the contribution
of FISH to our cytogenetic classification, we allowed extrapolation of FISH results for
primary cytogenetic abnormalities only (i.e., patients were considered positive for primary
IgH translocations and hyperdiploidy, if they were positive by FISH at any point during the
course of disease). In contrast, patients were considered positive for secondary
cytogenetic abnormalities (gain or amplification of chr1q/1q+, del13q, and del17p), if a
positive FISH result was obtained at baseline or prior to that. Positive results for
secondary abnormalities that were obtained after treatment administration were not
considered to account for the possibility of a newly acquired secondary abnormality.
To identify cytogenetic biomarkers of biochemical progression, we combined
extrapolated FISH results with results from scRNAseq and WGS (which were conducted
on tumor cells from a total of 19 patients who had tumor cells available for testing). We
restricted this analysis to patients with SMM and cytogenetic classification (n=35) and
tested only abnormalities that were present in at least 2 patients (primary: t(11;14), t(4;14),
t(14;16), hyperdiploidy; secondary: 1q+, del13q, del17p) using Cox regression and two-
sided Wald tests. Kaplan-Meier analyses with two-sided log-rank tests were also
conducted for cytogenetic abnormalities with a two-sided Wald p < 0.05.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this study by Nadeem et al, the investigators tried to address whether early intervention with daratumumab can improve
outcomes in patients with high-risk monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (HR-MGUS) and low-risk
smoldering multiple myeloma (LR-SMM). The authors enrolled 41 patients and achieved a 54% overall response rate with
17% deep responses. At a median follow-up of ~5 years, 2 patients (~5%) progressed to MM.
First, I have the following major concerns regarding the overall study design:
1. The primary endpoint of this trial is not clinically meaningful. The hematologic response assessment in multiple myeloma
as per the IMWG criteria has never been validated in this population (HR-MGUS and LR-SMM). As the authors themselves
show in Figure 3 (A and B), achieving VGPR or better was not significantly associated with SLiM-CRAB PFS despite long
follow-up. It was only associated with biochemical PFS, the clinical importance of which is unclear in this population.
2. The authors have devised a cytogenetic risk score for biochemical PFS. I would strongly suggest to remove it from the
manuscript due to the following reasons:
a) The outcome being predicted by this risk score is not clinically meaningful.
b) This dataset is not powered for any multivariable analysis, and the best practices for devising a clinical risk prediction
score (e.g. taking all available important variables into account, assessing discrimination and calibration etc.) were not
followed.
The authors can simply report descriptively the prognostic impact of each cytogenetic abnormality on univariate analysis.
Other major comments:
1. The authors must clearly state in the abstract and the 1st paragraph of the discussion that the study failed to achieve its
primary endpoint.
2. Two patients in this cohort progressed to MM, both based on SLiM criteria. In the patient with sFLC ratio>100, was a 24
hour urine Bence Jones protein obtained at baseline prior to induction therapy? If so, please provide that information.
3. The authors should provide data on the time-interval between date of original diagnosis of HR-MGUS/LR-SMM and
enrollment in this trial.
Minor comments:
1. In the introduction, the authors should clarify what is the expected risk of progression to MM in patients with HR-MGUS
and LR-SMM as the criteria used in this trial.
2. In the discussion (Page 6-7), the authors state that “Here, we demonstrated for the first time that depth of response also
matters in patients with a lower risk of progression, and therefore, this should be considered in the end-points of future
clinical trials of SMM.” I think this is extremely premature, and is not borne out of the data presented in this trial, which shows
that depth of response was only correlated with biochemical PFS but not SLiM-CRAB PFS.
